claims.text: Principles 6 (Customers' interests), 7 (Communications with clients), 8 (Conflicts of interest), 9 (Customers: relationships of trust), 10 (Clients' assets) and 12 (Consumer Duty) impose requirements on firms expressly in relation to their clients or customers, with the requirements depending in part on the characteristics of the client or customer concerned.
A firm must act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers (Principle 12 - Consumer Duty).
The cross-cutting obligations at PRIN 2A.2 set out the overarching conduct which firms must demonstrate when they act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers.

Principle 12 does not change the nature of a firm's relationship with any given retail customer; it does not create a fiduciary relationship where one would not otherwise exist nor require a firm to provide advice or carry out any other regulated activity where it would not otherwise have done so.

The FCA has issued guidance on the Consumer Duty in FG22/5, which firms should read alongside Principle 12 and PRIN 2A as a guide to the FCA's view as to how Principle 12 and PRIN 2A might be complied with.
Principle 12 imposes obligations on firms towards retail customers of products irrespective of whether the customer is a client of the firm.
Obligations on firms in the distribution chain of a product must be interpreted reasonably, in a manner that reflects the firm's role in that distribution chain.
The extent of a firm's responsibilities under Principle 12 in any one case will turn on the substance of the firm's role in the arrangements relating to the product.
Given the high-level nature and breadth of application of the Principles, guidance about a Principle cannot exhaustively cover its implications.
Principle 12 imposes a higher and more exacting standard of conduct in relation to a firm's retail market business relative to what Principles 6 or 7 would have otherwise required.
The application of Principles 6 and 7 is unchanged with respect to a firm's activities insofar as they are not subject to Principle 12.
A firm must act in good faith towards retail customers.
A firm must avoid causing foreseeable harm to retail customers.

Foreseeable harm may be caused by both act and omission, in a firm's direct relationship with a retail customer or through its role in the distribution chain even where another firm in that chain also contributes to the harm.

Avoiding causing foreseeable harm includes ensuring all aspects of design, terms, marketing, sale and support for products avoid causing foreseeable harm, and ensuring no aspect of business involves unfairly exploiting behavioural biases or vulnerability characteristics.
A firm with an ongoing relationship with a retail customer in relation to a product would need to act to avoid causing foreseeable harm to that customer throughout the lifecycle of that product.

limitations: HARD_INVOICE_CAP_NOT_GUARANTEED: enforcement is pre-flight reserve + post-hoc token accounting — not Anthropic billing API.
Pricing uses static MODEL_PRICING_ESTIMATE — actual Anthropic invoice may differ.
Per-process overlap lock does not synchronise across Vercel serverless instances; the database allows one RUNNING UC-RI-005 run per organisation.
Duplicate idempotency keys always reuse the existing run; a new paid attempt requires a new operator-authorised RI_LAB_TRIAL_IDEMPOTENCY_SUFFIX.
A request that passes pre-flight may still consume thinking tokens inside max_tokens before text appears; partial responses may still incur billed input tokens.
No org-wide Anthropic workspace spend cap — only per-request guard when env is set.
Retries inside callAnthropicMessages are not implemented; retryReserveFactor reserves headroom only.
Provider errors after HTTP 200 may still bill input/output tokens reported by Anthropic.
